title: Why DDIM Hallucinates More Than DDPM: A Theoretical Analysis of Reverse Dynamics
claim: Deterministic sampling gets trapped in intermediate regions between modes and hallucinates, while added stochasticity lets trajectories escape to true modes.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: sample scatter plots, trajectory geometry, stacked trap-vs-escape diagrams
description: Three panels (a), (b), (c). Panel (a) shows two scatter plots of 100,000 samples from a 25-mode Gaussian mixture on a 5x5 grid: the left plot (DDPM) has samples clustered at the true modes (red stars), and the right plot (DDIM) has dense blue bridges along the segments between modes, which are the hallucinations. Panel (b) is a schematic square with four black mode points μ(1)–μ(4). Purple noisy start points x_T and x'_T give blue and red trajectories that converge on the segment L(2,4). One ends at the true mode μ(2), circled in green. The other ends at the segment midpoint y*, circled in dashed red. Panel (c) has two stacked diagrams on a line between μ(i) and μ(j), each with an orange ϑ-neighborhood box. The red DDIM trajectory is trapped at the midpoint, labeled 'Trapped (mode interpolation)'. The green DDPM trajectory, labeled 'noise', crosses the box and escapes to the true mode. Red marks failure and green marks success.
caption: (a) In 100,000 generated samples for a 25-mode Gaussian mixture target, despite using the same pretrained model, DDPM (left) hallucinates significantly less than DDIM (right). (b) Towards the beginning of the reverse process, the trajectory selects a line segment to converge to. After that, the trajectory converges rapidly to the nearest line segment: either the true mode or the midpoint neighborhood. (c) Within the midpoint neighborhood, DDIM can get stuck and hallucinate, while DDPM can escape with added noise and avoid hallucination.
abstract: We theoretically study the hallucination phenomena in two canonical diffusion samplers: the stochastic Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) and the deterministic Denoising Diffusion Implicit Model (DDIM). We analyze the reverse ODE (DDIM) and SDE (DDPM) for a Gaussian mixture target, proving that after a critical time $Ï$, (a) DDIM can become stuck on the segment connecting the two nearest modes and (b) DDPM *stochasticity* helps it become unstuck from this region, thus avoiding hallucination. Our empirical validation verifies that DDPM has a significantly lower hallucination rate than DDIM when this region is entered. Building on our observations, we exhibit how using additional stochastic steps can help DDIM avoid hallucinations and offer new insights on how to design improved samplers.
